questions.question: What is a Dockerfile and what are the key instructions?
questions.direct_answer: A Dockerfile is a text build definition that turns a base image and build context into an image. Common instructions are `FROM`, `WORKDIR`, `COPY`, `RUN`, `ARG`, `ENV`, `USER`, `EXPOSE`, `ENTRYPOINT`, and `CMD`. Instructions affect filesystem state or image metadata, but it is inaccurate to say every instruction creates a filesystem layer.
follow_up_questions: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in Dockerfile?

sections.title: Dockerfile Basics and Layer-Based Image Building
sections.content:
A **Dockerfile** is a plain text script that tells Docker how to build an image — think of it as a recipe for creating a containerized version of your application. Each line in a Dockerfile is an **instruction** that Docker executes step by step, and each instruction creates a new **layer** in the final image.

Layers stack on top of each other like transparent sheets: the base operating system at the bottom, then your JDK, then your application JAR, then configuration. **Why layers matter**: Docker caches each layer. If you rebuild and nothing changed in a layer, Docker reuses the cached version instead of rebuilding it. This is why you put stable things (like base images and dependencies) early in the Dockerfile and frequently changing things (like your compiled JAR) near the end. For a Spring Boot app, you typically start from a lightweight Java base image like **eclipse-temurin:17-jre**, set up your working directory, copy the JAR file, and define the startup command. The analogy: building a Dockerfile is like making a layered cake — each ingredient goes in at the right step, and you don't remix the whole batter every time you add frosting on top.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Dockerfile|~Recipe for an image|plain text instructions|read top to bottom|each line is a layer
blue|Core Instructions|~The essentials|FROM base image|COPY the JAR|ENTRYPOINT to run
emerald|Build and Run|~From file to running|docker build -t app .|docker run -p 8080:8080|EXPOSE is just docs
violet|Layer Order|~Cache-friendly|stable steps first|JAR copy last|fast rebuilds

sections.title: Spring Boot Dockerfile with Key Instructions
sections.content:
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY target/order-service-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar app.jar

EXPOSE 8080

ENV SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

sections.title: When to Write a Dockerfile
sections.content:
Use a Dockerfile when you need to **package your Spring Boot application for consistent deployment** across different environments. If your app runs fine on your laptop but breaks on the test server due to different Java versions or missing dependencies, a Dockerfile solves that by locking in the exact runtime environment.

Use it when deploying to **Kubernetes, AWS ECS, or any cloud platform** that runs containers — these platforms pull your Docker image and run it identically everywhere. Also use it when you need to **version your entire runtime stack** alongside your code: base OS, JDK version, environment variables, and startup command all live in one versioned file. Finally, write a Dockerfile when you want **fast onboarding for new developers** — they can run docker build and docker run without installing Java, Maven, or configuring local databases.

sections.title: Common Dockerfile Mistakes Freshers Make
sections.content:
- **Too many layers from separate RUN commands**: Running apt-get update in one RUN and apt-get install in another creates two layers instead of one. Combine related commands with && to reduce layers: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl.
- **Copying everything before dependencies**: If you COPY the entire project directory first, then run mvn package, Docker invalidates the cache every time any file changes. Instead, copy pom.xml first, run mvn dependency:go-offline to cache dependencies, then copy source code.
- **Not using multi-stage builds for Spring Boot**: Freshers often copy the target JAR from their local machine into the image. Better: use a multi-stage Dockerfile that runs mvn package inside a builder stage, then copies only the final JAR to a slim runtime stage, avoiding bloated images with Maven and source code.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `FROM` chooses a base or begins a new build stage.
- `WORKDIR`, `COPY`, and `RUN` set context and produce build results.
- `ARG` is build-time input; `ENV` records environment defaults in image configuration.
- `USER`, `EXPOSE`, `ENTRYPOINT`, and `CMD` configure runtime behavior/metadata.
- Use `.dockerignore`, pinned/trusted bases, non-root execution, and cache-aware ordering; not every instruction adds filesystem data.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Dockerfile is a text build definition for creating an image from a base and a build context. `FROM` selects a base or starts a new stage. `WORKDIR` sets the working directory, `COPY` adds context files, and `RUN` executes a build step. `ARG` provides build-time input, while `ENV` records environment defaults. `USER`, `EXPOSE`, `ENTRYPOINT`, and `CMD` configure runtime behavior or metadata.

For a Spring Boot service I can use a JDK build stage to test and package the JAR, then copy it into a smaller runtime stage, set a non-root user, and use exec-form `ENTRYPOINT`. A `.dockerignore` keeps irrelevant files out of the build context.

Not every instruction creates a filesystem layer—some change image configuration. I also avoid baking secrets into `ARG`, `ENV`, or `RUN`, pin trusted base images, combine package-manager update/install safely, and rebuild the image rather than editing a live container.

questions.question: What is a .dockerignore file and why is it important?
questions.direct_answer: `.dockerignore` removes matching paths from the build context sent to the builder. This can reduce transfer and cache invalidation and can stop an accidental `COPY . .` from seeing local files. It does not automatically shrink an image whose Dockerfile never copied those files, and it is not a secret-management boundary.
follow_up_questions: How do you include a specific file while excluding its parent directory in .dockerignore?
What are the security implications of including .env in a Docker image?

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Patterns filter the build context before Dockerfile `COPY`/`ADD` can use it.
- A smaller context can transfer faster and invalidate fewer cache results.
- Ignore VCS data, build output, local caches, and files the build does not need.
- The final image is smaller only when excluded files would otherwise have been copied.
- Do not rely on `.dockerignore` for secrets; use BuildKit secret mounts and credential controls.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`.dockerignore` filters paths from the build context before it is sent to the builder. That means a normal `COPY` or `ADD` cannot see a matching file from that context.

For a Java project I might exclude `.git`, local IDE files, logs, and existing build output when the container build produces its own artifact. This can reduce context transfer and stop irrelevant file changes invalidating a broad `COPY . .` step. It reduces final image size only if those files would otherwise be copied.

I do not treat it as a secret boundary. Credentials can still leak through build arguments, logs, a different context, or an explicit override. BuildKit secret mounts are the better pattern for a private Maven token needed during one `RUN` step. The file should be tested against the actual Dockerfile so it does not exclude the wrapper, source, or artifact the build needs.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
The **build context** is the set of files made available to the builder. `.dockerignore` is evaluated before those files are sent, so a matching file cannot be read by a normal `COPY` or `ADD` from that context.

This improves builds in two ways: fewer bytes are transferred, and irrelevant changes—such as `.git` data or local logs—do not keep invalidating a broad `COPY . .` step. It only changes image size if the Dockerfile would otherwise copy those files.

Treat it as hygiene, not a secret vault. Credentials may leak through build arguments, command history, logs, another context, or a deliberate override. BuildKit secret mounts provide sensitive data to a build step without baking it into the final layer when used correctly.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Build Context|~Sent to the daemon|whole dir by default|.git, target, IDE files|can be 100s of MB
blue|.dockerignore|~Filter the context|works like .gitignore|patterns and ! negation|exclude the noise
emerald|Why It Matters|~Speed plus size|faster build start|smaller images|less to upload
violet|Security|~Keep secrets out|exclude .env and keys|else baked in layers|docker history exposes them

sections.title: When to Use a .dockerignore File
sections.content:
Use a .dockerignore file **in every project with a Dockerfile** — it should be as automatic as adding a .gitignore.

Use it when you notice slow build times because Docker is uploading hundreds of megabytes before it even starts building. For Spring Boot apps, if you run mvn package locally before docker build, the target/ directory contains all your compiled classes and the fat JAR — you don't need those in the build context since you'll COPY only the final JAR.

Use .dockerignore to **protect secrets and local config** from leaking into images: exclude .env files, id_rsa keys, kubeconfig, and local application-dev.yml files.

Use it to **reduce image size**: if your Dockerfile has COPY . /app, any file not in .dockerignore ends up in the image, including test code, documentation, and Git history. Excluding those keeps your production image lean. Finally, use .dockerignore when **building in CI/CD pipelines** where the build context is cloned from Git — excluding .git/ alone saves hundreds of megabytes of history data from being sent to Docker.

sections.title: Common .dockerignore Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not creating one at all**: Freshers skip .dockerignore entirely and wonder why docker build takes 30 seconds just to send context. Without it, Docker uploads every file in the directory, including target/ with 200MB of dependencies and class files.
- **Excluding the JAR you need**: Freshers copy their entire .gitignore into .dockerignore, which excludes target/ containing the JAR. If your Dockerfile says COPY target/app.jar, the build fails because target/ is ignored. Solution: exclude target/ in .dockerignore but COPY target/*.jar explicitly before building the image, or build the JAR inside a multi-stage Docker build.
- **Not excluding .env files**: Local environment files with database passwords or API keys get copied into the image if not explicitly excluded. These secrets then persist in image layers even if deleted later — anyone with access to the image can extract them using docker history.

sections.title: Spring Boot Dockerfile with Key Instructions
sections.content:
```text
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY target/order-service-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar app.jar

EXPOSE 8080

ENV SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: ENTRYPOINT defines the main executable that always runs when the container starts, while CMD provides default arguments to that executable. If you specify both, CMD becomes the arguments to ENTRYPOINT. CMD can be easily overridden by passing arguments to docker run, but ENTRYPOINT requires the --entrypoint flag to override.

questions.question: How do you pass environment variables to a Spring Boot app running in Docker?
questions.direct_answer: At runtime, pass configuration with `docker run -e NAME=value`, `--env-file`, Compose `environment`/`env_file`, or mounted configuration. Spring Boot maps environment names such as `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` into its `Environment` using relaxed binding and precedence rules. Do not put long-lived secrets directly in image `ENV`, source-controlled Compose files, or command history.
follow_up_questions: What is the 12-factor app methodology and how does it relate to env var configuration?
Why should you not put secrets directly in environment variables in production?

sections.title: Environment Variables for Spring Boot in Docker
sections.content:
Spring Boot applications read configuration from **application.properties** or **application.yml** at startup, but hardcoding values like database URLs or API keys in those files doesn't work in containerized environments where configuration changes between dev, test, and production. The solution is **environment variables**, which you pass into the container at runtime using the **-e flag** with docker run or the **environment section** in docker-compose.yml. Spring Boot has a feature called **relaxed binding** that automatically maps environment variables to properties: SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL becomes spring.datasource.url.

This means you can externalize all environment-specific configuration without touching your application code or properties files. The pattern: keep sensible defaults in application.yml (like spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb for local dev), then override them with environment variables in production. Docker makes this seamless — your image stays the same, but the runtime behavior changes based on the environment variables you inject. For a Spring Boot app connecting to PostgreSQL, you'd run docker run -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/orders -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=admin -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=secret myapp. Spring Boot reads those variables and overrides the defaults. This approach is essential in **cloud-native deployments** where configuration comes from Kubernetes ConfigMaps or AWS Secrets Manager.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Pass at Runtime|~Configure containers|docker run -e KEY=VALUE|--env-file .env|compose environment block
blue|Relaxed Binding|~Auto property mapping|SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL|maps to spring.datasource.url|uppercase plus underscores
emerald|Override Defaults|~Env beats properties|one image, many envs|dev = staging = prod|just change vars
violet|Secrets|~Never in Dockerfile ENV|baked into the image|docker inspect leaks it|use a secrets manager

sections.title: Passing Environment Variables to Spring Boot Container
sections.content:
docker run -d \
  --name order-service \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://postgres-db:5432/orders \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=orderuser \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=secret123 \
  -e SERVER_PORT=8080 \
  order-service:latest

# In docker-compose.yml:
services:
  order-service:
    image: order-service:latest
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres-db:5432/orders
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: orderuser
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: secret123
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

sections.title: When to Use Environment Variables for Configuration
sections.content:
Use environment variables **whenever configuration changes between environments** — database URLs, API endpoints, credentials, feature flags, and logging levels should all be environment variables, not hardcoded in application.properties.

Use them when **deploying to cloud platforms** like AWS, Azure, or Kubernetes, where configuration is injected at runtime from services like AWS Secrets Manager or Kubernetes ConfigMaps.

Use environment variables for **secrets management**: never commit passwords or API keys to Git, even in application.properties. Instead, pass them as environment variables at runtime so they stay out of your source code and Docker image layers.

Use them in **CI/CD pipelines** where the same Docker image needs to run in dev, staging, and production with different configs — you build once, deploy everywhere, varying only the environment variables.

Use Spring Boot's **relaxed binding** for clean mapping: SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL automatically becomes spring.datasource.url, so you don't need custom code to read environment variables. Finally, use environment variables when you need **runtime flexibility** — changing a config value is as simple as restarting the container with new -e flags, no need to rebuild the image.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with Environment Variables in Docker
sections.content:
- **Hardcoding production config in application.properties**: Freshers put spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://prod-db:5432/orders directly in the properties file, meaning the same image can't run in dev or test environments without rebuilding. Use environment variables instead and keep only dev defaults in properties files.
- **Not using relaxed binding**: Freshers manually read environment variables with System.getenv("DB_URL") and set properties programmatically. Spring Boot already does this automatically — just use standard naming like SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL and it maps to spring.datasource.url.
- **Passing secrets in Dockerfile with ENV**: Writing ENV SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=secret123 in the Dockerfile bakes the secret into the image layer permanently, visible to anyone who pulls the image. Pass secrets at runtime with -e or from a secrets manager, never in the Dockerfile.
- **Forgetting spring.profiles.active**: Freshers pass database config but forget to activate the production profile with -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod, so Spring Boot still loads dev configuration from application-dev.yml.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `docker run -e` and `--env-file` provide runtime environment values.
- Compose supports `environment` and `env_file`; orchestration platforms also support mounted config/secrets.
- Spring Boot relaxed binding maps canonical property names to uppercase underscore environment names.
- Environment values usually override packaged config data, but Spring Boot has a full ordered property-source model.
- Use a secret manager or mounted secret/config tree for sensitive values; environment inspection can expose them.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I provide Spring Boot runtime configuration through the container environment or mounted configuration rather than rebuilding one image per environment. With Docker I can use `-e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=...` or `--env-file`; Compose offers `environment` and `env_file`. Spring Boot's relaxed binding maps the uppercase underscore form to the canonical property name.

For example, `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` can override a default from packaged configuration according to Spring Boot's property-source precedence. For groups of values or sensitive data, a mounted configuration tree or the target platform's config/secret mechanism may be clearer.

Environment values are visible to processes and inspection paths with sufficient access, and command-line values can remain in shell history. I therefore do not bake passwords into Dockerfile `ENV` or commit them to Compose. I validate required values at startup and consult the full Spring Boot precedence model instead of assuming every external value wins in every situation.

questions.question: What do the ENV, WORKDIR, and EXPOSE instructions do in a Dockerfile?
questions.title: ENV, WORKDIR, and EXPOSE in Dockerfile
questions.direct_answer: `WORKDIR` sets the working directory for later Dockerfile instructions and the default container process, creating it if needed. `ENV` adds environment defaults to image configuration and affects later build instructions and containers unless overridden. `EXPOSE` documents intended listening ports; it does not publish them to the host.

sections.title: Understanding WORKDIR, ENV, and EXPOSE in Dockerfiles
sections.content:
These three instructions appear in nearly every production Dockerfile, and understanding their behavior is essential for writing correct and maintainable images. **WORKDIR** sets the working directory inside the container — think of it as running cd /app inside the container. All subsequent COPY, RUN, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT instructions execute relative to this directory.

If the directory doesn't exist, Docker creates it automatically. Without WORKDIR, commands run from the root directory /, which is messy and error-prone. **ENV** sets environment variables that persist into the running container. Variables defined with ENV are available to your application at runtime. For a Spring Boot app, you might set ENV SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod in the Dockerfile, and Spring Boot reads that variable when it starts. **EXPOSE** documents which port your application listens on, like EXPOSE 8080. It's purely **metadata** for documentation and tooling — it does not actually open or publish the port to the host machine. You still need the **-p flag** with docker run (like -p 8080:8080) to map the container port to the host. Think of EXPOSE as a hint to future developers or orchestration tools like Docker Compose or Kubernetes about which port to publish.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|WORKDIR|~Sets the working dir|like cd into /app|creates it if missing|COPY and RUN go relative
blue|ENV|~Runtime env vars|SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE|persists in container|overridable with -e
emerald|EXPOSE|~Documents the port|metadata only|does NOT publish|need -p to map it
violet|ENV vs ARG|~Know the scope|ENV is runtime|ARG is build-time only|no secrets in ENV

sections.title: Using WORKDIR, ENV, and EXPOSE in a Spring Boot Dockerfile
sections.content:
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY target/payment-service-1.0.0.jar app.jar

ENV SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
ENV JAVA_OPTS="-Xmx512m -Xms256m"

EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["sh", "-c", "java $JAVA_OPTS -jar app.jar"]

sections.title: When to Use WORKDIR, ENV, and EXPOSE
sections.content:
Use **WORKDIR** at the start of your Dockerfile to set a clean working directory like /app or /usr/src/app, so all file operations happen in one predictable location. This avoids cluttering the root directory and makes paths in COPY and RUN commands clearer.

Use **ENV** to set environment variables that your application needs at runtime, like Spring profiles, JVM options, or paths to configuration files. ENV is also useful for defining variables used later in the Dockerfile itself, like ENV APP_VERSION=1.0.0. Remember that ENV values can be overridden at runtime with docker run -e, which makes them good for configuration that might change between environments.

Use **EXPOSE** to document which port your Spring Boot app listens on, typically 8080. Tools like Docker Compose and Kubernetes read the EXPOSE instruction to automatically publish ports, and it helps other developers understand your container without digging through application code. However, EXPOSE alone doesn't do anything functional — you must use -p 8080:8080 when running the container to actually map the port to the host.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with WORKDIR, ENV, and EXPOSE
sections.content:
- **Not using WORKDIR**: Freshers skip WORKDIR and use absolute paths like COPY target/app.jar /app/app.jar, then RUN commands fail because the working directory is still /. Always set WORKDIR early so subsequent commands use relative paths.
- **Thinking EXPOSE publishes the port**: The biggest mistake is believing EXPOSE 8080 makes the container accessible on localhost:8080. It doesn't. EXPOSE is documentation only. You must use docker run -p 8080:8080 to actually map the port. Without -p, the container runs but the port isn't reachable from the host.
- **Hardcoding secrets in ENV**: Freshers write ENV DB_PASSWORD=secret123 in the Dockerfile, baking the secret into the image. Anyone who pulls the image can see it with docker history. Use ENV for non-sensitive config only, and pass secrets at runtime with docker run -e.
- **Overusing ENV for build-time variables**: ENV persists into the running container. If you only need a variable during the build, use ARG instead of ENV to avoid cluttering the runtime environment.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `WORKDIR /app` sets a path for later `RUN`, `COPY`, `CMD`, and `ENTRYPOINT` behavior.
- `ENV KEY=value` persists a default in image metadata and can be overridden at runtime.
- Do not put secrets in `ENV`; image metadata is inspectable.
- `EXPOSE 8080` documents a container port and helps `-P`, but creates no host mapping.
- Use `docker run -p ...` or Compose `ports` to publish a port.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`WORKDIR` sets the working directory for later instructions such as `RUN`, `COPY`, `CMD`, and `ENTRYPOINT`, and creates the directory if needed. A later `FROM` begins a new stage and resets stage-specific context unless it is set again.

`ENV NAME=value` stores an environment default in image configuration. It affects later build steps and containers created from the image, but runtime `-e` or platform configuration can override it. Because image metadata is inspectable, I never use Dockerfile `ENV` for a secret.

`EXPOSE 8080` documents that the image expects a service on a container port and supports behaviors such as `docker run -P`; it does not create a host listener. I still publish explicitly with `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080` or Compose `ports` when host access is required.

questions.question: What is the difference between ENTRYPOINT and CMD in a Dockerfile?
questions.direct_answer: In exec-form usage, `ENTRYPOINT` defines the executable and `CMD` supplies default arguments when both are present. With only `CMD`, it defines the default command. Arguments after the image name replace `CMD`; `--entrypoint` replaces `ENTRYPOINT`. Shell-form instructions have different argument and signal behavior, so exec form is usually clearer for services.
follow_up_questions: What is the exec form vs shell form in ENTRYPOINT?
How do you pass JVM flags like -Xmx in a Docker ENTRYPOINT?

sections.title: Container Startup Commands: ENTRYPOINT vs CMD
sections.content:
Both **ENTRYPOINT** and **CMD** define what command runs when a Docker container starts, but they serve different purposes and behave differently when combined. **ENTRYPOINT** specifies the fixed command that always executes — think of it as the main program your container runs, like java -jar for a Spring Boot app. **CMD** provides default arguments to that command, which can be easily overridden at runtime. When you use both together, ENTRYPOINT is the executable and CMD supplies its default parameters.

The key difference: CMD is completely replaced if you pass arguments to docker run, while ENTRYPOINT stays put unless you explicitly override it with the --entrypoint flag. This design lets you build flexible containers where the core behavior (ENTRYPOINT) is locked but users can customize arguments (CMD) without rebuilding the image. For a Spring Boot application, you'd typically set ENTRYPOINT to ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"] and CMD to default Spring profiles or JVM options, so developers can override those options when running the container locally versus in production.

sections.title: Key Ideas at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|ENTRYPOINT|~Fixed executable|always runs|java -jar app.jar|needs --entrypoint to override
blue|CMD|~Default arguments|or full command alone|replaced by run args|the flexible part
emerald|Together|~ENTRYPOINT plus CMD|exec plus default flags|run args replace CMD|java -jar stays put
violet|Exec Form|~Use the brackets|java comma -jar form|runs as PID 1|SIGTERM reaches the app

sections.title: ENTRYPOINT + CMD in a Spring Boot Dockerfile
sections.content:
```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/order-service.jar app.jar

# ENTRYPOINT = fixed executable; CMD = default args you can override at run time
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
CMD ["--spring.profiles.active=prod"]

# docker run order-service
#   -> java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
# docker run order-service --spring.profiles.active=dev
#   -> CMD replaced; java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev
# Use exec form (brackets) so Java is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM cleanly.
```

sections.title: When to Use ENTRYPOINT vs CMD
sections.content:
Use **ENTRYPOINT alone** when your container has one specific job that should never change, like a database container that always runs postgres or a Spring Boot app that always runs java -jar app.jar.

Use **CMD alone** when you want maximum flexibility — the entire command can be replaced at runtime, useful for utility images like a Maven image where you might run mvn clean package one time and mvn test another.

Use **ENTRYPOINT with CMD together** when you want a fixed core command but flexible arguments: ENTRYPOINT is your executable (java -jar app.jar) and CMD is the default configuration (like --spring.profiles.active=dev). This pattern is ideal for Spring Boot apps because you can run the container with default settings in development, then override CMD with production profiles in Kubernetes.

Use **exec form syntax** ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"] instead of shell form java -jar app.jar to ensure proper signal handling — shell form wraps your command in /bin/sh -c, making it PID 2 instead of PID 1, so SIGTERM signals don't reach your Java process for graceful shutdown.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with ENTRYPOINT and CMD
sections.content:
- **Using CMD when ENTRYPOINT is better**: Freshers often write CMD ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"] thinking it locks down the startup command, but any argument passed to docker run replaces the entire CMD. If someone runs docker run myapp /bin/bash, your Java app never starts. Use ENTRYPOINT for fixed commands.
- **Mixing exec form and shell form**: Writing ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar"] with CMD app.jar (without brackets) creates a type mismatch. Both must use exec form ["..."] or both shell form.
- **Not understanding argument replacement**: Freshers think docker run myapp --spring.profiles.active=prod appends to CMD, but it replaces CMD entirely. If your ENTRYPOINT is java -jar app.jar, you'd need to pass the JAR name again. Solution: put the JAR in ENTRYPOINT and only profiles in CMD.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `CMD` alone supplies the default command.
- With exec-form `ENTRYPOINT`, `CMD` becomes its default arguments.
- Arguments after the image name replace `CMD`.
- `--entrypoint` replaces the configured entrypoint.
- Prefer exec form for predictable argument combination and signal delivery; shell form behaves differently.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`CMD` supplies a container's default command when used alone. When an exec-form `ENTRYPOINT` is also present, `CMD` supplies its default arguments. Arguments after the image name replace `CMD`, while `docker run --entrypoint ...` replaces the entrypoint.

For example, `ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","/app/app.jar"]` with `CMD ["--spring.profiles.active=prod"]` runs the JAR with that default profile. `docker run image --spring.profiles.active=dev` replaces only the CMD argument.

Exec and shell forms matter. Exec form avoids an extra shell and generally gives the application clearer signal behavior. Shell form changes argument combination and PID/signal handling. I use ENTRYPOINT for a stable executable and CMD for replaceable defaults, but either instruction can be overridden; ENTRYPOINT is not an unbreakable command.
